title: Rocket Science

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: It’s not often a boyhood dream comes true, especially if that dream is to launch rockets into space. But that’s what’s happened for New Zealand rocket enthusiast Peter Beck. And, says Beck, New Zealand is the perfect place for launching satellites into space because there’s limited air traffic, a small population, infrequent shipping and generally it is very remote. By contrast, in the USA, launches would be restricted by the concentration of flights, shipping and people. Admittedly, Beck didn’t always see it this way. In 2007 he packed his bags for the trip of a lifetime to visit aerospace companies in the USA. ‘I started talking to these guys and they go, “You don’t want to work here.”’ I realised that I was just going to be a tiny gear in a giant bureaucratic machine.’ Depressed, he caught the plane home, but even on the flight he’d decided his new company name and logo and, six months later, he set up Rocketlab. Beck makes it sound easy, but soon he plans to send his first payload into space. After that, he says, there are 30 or so customers lined up. There’ll be one launch a month the following year and one a week the year after that.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Beck can be impatient with what he sees as the lack of scientific knowledge. ‘Nobody thinks of themselves as living in a solar system,’ he complains. ‘If you ask the average person to name the planets, they can’t.’ But for Beck, space has always mattered. He built his own telescope as a child, inspired by his father, who was an engineer and later a museum director. Aged about seven, Peter’s father took him to a meeting of the Astronomical Society, whose members talked about space and telescopes. Peter recalls being absolutely fascinated, though he could probably make sense of just 5% of what was being said. Beck’s love of engineering continued at technical college, where the metalwork teacher gave him the keys to the workshop, so he could work in the evenings and at weekends.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The same was true when he started work as a tool-making apprentice for engineers Fisher & Paykel. Here, with help from his colleagues, he built a rocket-powered bicycle which reached speeds of 140 kph. Next, Beck secured a job at Industrial Research Ltd., whose building manager Alan Johnston says, ‘Lots of people have a passion for things and don’t follow through. Peter’s passion is rockets – but he’s also got engineering skills. He can see it through to completion.’ Another early supporter was the internet entrepreneur and space enthusiast Mark Stevens. Beck approached Stevens and the two hit it off, with the latter becoming a 50% owner of Rocketlab. ‘That’s because we had a similar vision,’ explains Stevens. ‘We believe a space industry can emerge from New Zealand.’ Stevens went on to receive global media coverage as the first New Zealander to join Virgin Galactic’s space tourism programme.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The pair attracted another supporter, the merchant banker Sir Michael Fay, whose private island, Great Mercury, lies off the New Zealand coast. Says Beck, ‘We asked Sir Michael if we could launch off his island, and he just said, ‘Anything you need, you’ve got.’ He gave us use of his helicopter, house, chef, and as a result we could do demonstration launches to really influential people – it was remarkable,’ recalls Beck. Support has come from other sources as well, even the bureaucrats at Civil Aviation. ‘What’s more,’ says Beck, ‘we talked to central Government and they’ve always bent over backwards and helped us.’ The work came to a climax with the first launch of Atea 1, Rocketlab’s prototype rocket. ‘It was an amazing sight…,’ Stevens wrote. ‘The spectators were elated and tears of joy erupted.’ They all watched in wonder as the rocket flew powerfully into the sky.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Rocketlab today is a plain, concrete office building near Auckland airport. It hardly looks like the headquarters of a pioneering satellite company. In fact, a similar organisation in the USA would almost certainly have very heavy security, but here there’s hardly any evidence of such measures and it’s relatively easy to gain access. It makes Rocketlab’s success all the more remarkable. With just three staff in 2010, the firm won contracts with international firms for aerospace work, and since then that number has increased, along with the number of investors. Beck wanted to take a new approach, ‘…to start from scratch and assume there were no constraints.’ He says that most rockets are built by taking an old motor from one space programme, a fuel tank from another, and putting all these parts together. So he went back to the drawing board and the result is Electron, which has carbon-fibre construction and high-tech electronics, meaning it will be much cheaper to launch than any previous rocket built by other companies. One important consequence of this is that the long-anticipated shift from government-dominated space travel to programmes which industry is funding and managing might actually now happen. And in the meantime, Electron keeps winning impressive support.
